title: Townies
logline: Labor Day weekend, Cal crosses Mill Street into the town that hates the school, finds a bar with a long memory, and learns what the oldest house on Elm Row does when somebody stops breathing.
previously: CAL (to Priya, holding her phone): "Priya. Is this you?"
CAL: "Delete it. And you tell Dev. Tomorrow. Before breakfast." PRIYA: "He's going to be nice about it. That's the worst part."
CAL (at the Rho, aloud, to a silent chapter room): "T. C." BROOKS: "Nobody says them out loud."
MARGAUX (crossing the lawn): "Hello, Whitaker. Your photographer took the day off."
BROOKS (in his own voice): "Stay in English. He'll respect it in about thirty years." RICHARD (by text): "Brooks says you signed. Proud of you."
PRIYA (at his door): "You asked me if I was writing about you. I was. Now I'm writing about me." CAL: "Come in."
calNow: Cal has signed his father's name into a silver cup, named the girl who watched his window, and swum out to pull a teammate off a buoy that wouldn't hold still. He is publicly with Margaux and privately waiting at 3:07 for a post that never comes. His father didn't call, and the one who spoke for him won't say why he sleeps with every light on.

cast.name: Priya Raman
cast.impression: Your self-appointed emergency contact, and the one behind @lowell.three. You followed her wet footprints, found the account open on her phone, and asked her to her face. She told you everything, deleted it, and told Dev before breakfast as you asked. Then she sat against your door until you came in. 'I'm going to be very annoying about this for a long time.' Her solo was approved, and she knows you vouched for it.

cast.name: Dev Okafor
cast.impression: The nicest guy on campus. When Priya told him everything at breakfast he asked if she'd eaten and pushed her half his toast. He had guessed you knew ('like she was a test you'd already seen the answers to') and said 'It's fine.' He sat in the hall with her and a plate of toast until you came home. His Tuesdays are still his own.

cast.name: Yusuf Haddad
cast.impression: Eleven words a day, all of them devastating. He brought coffee, a device name under a Post-it, and the offer to keep not knowing. He won't tell Dev.

cast.name: Nora Castellanos
cast.impression: Sharp, fair and your editing partner. She handed you a page of black marker bars; you wrote 'Not reading under it'; she wrote 'Noted' and told you to write your third sentence. She still keeps her own room closed.

cast.name: Danny Doyle
cast.role: High-school junior · Busboy at Dot's Diner
cast.impression: A seventeen-year-old busboy at Dot's with a pencil behind his ear and a side hustle he offered a total stranger. You bought what he was selling. He told you not to get caught, because his sister would kill him.

cast.name: Margaux Vance
cast.impression: Marble in daylight, someone else after dark, and now in public. She ordered your coffee without being told, counted out her own change in coins, and thanked you for not saying so. Across a lawn of phones she left Brooks's arm for yours and put a nickel in your palm. 'Now it's real. Now it's a picture.'

cast.name: Mae Sato
cast.impression: Headset, clipboard, deadpan. She read your nameplate and still calls you Pruitt, kept your name off the minutes, and decided your 'I meant it' makes the lie true retroactively. She wrote one word down.

cast.name: Simon Achterberg
cast.impression: Your guardian, camel coat and steamer. He dressed you in your father's blazer, tried it on himself ('Do I look like a Whitaker?'), and when you answered 'You look like my father' went still and took it off fast. He had already forgiven Priya.

cast.name: Prof. Helen Marsh
cast.impression: A voice like a paper cut. She read over your shoulder and asked, 'Whose voice is missing from this call?' You said 'Mine.' She said 'No.' and walked on.

cast.name: Brooks Hadley III
cast.role: Junior · Sigma Kappa Rho pledge master
cast.impression: Charming, watchful, quoting your father. He relayed Richard's message, then said 'Stay in English' in his own voice. He wrote down your swim time, handed you your father's pen, called you 'Brother' once over your father's bourbon, and told you the letters you spoke aloud are ones 'nobody says out loud.' He sleeps with every light on.

cast.name: Tommy Reyes
cast.impression: A hockey recruit from Worcester who is loud, loving and hiding something about the light. He told you 'There's two of the clock sometimes' and asked you not to tell coach. On the dock he lost the buoy and you went in after him. You were the only one who came.

cast.name: Richard Whitaker
cast.impression: Never on camera. He was supposed to call at 7:30 and didn't; Brooks 'handled it.' He texts 'Proud of you' to a signed card. He wants to talk properly at Trustee Weekend.

cast.name: Hollis Prescott
cast.impression: Square-jawed, gentle-voiced, a senator's grandson who makes brotherhood sound decent. His phone lights with one letter and he turns it face-down mid-sentence. When you said 'T. C.' he asked who that was, and seemed to mean it.

cast.name: Marcus Bell
cast.impression: A debater's smile, a clipboard and every rushee's swim time. 'I keep records.' He told you to sign 'on purpose' and watched the dock without writing.

cast.name: Augie Lindqvist
cast.impression: A golden-retriever freshman from Minnesota whose family makes combines. You agreed to pledge together: 'Buddy system.' He held your sleeve on the dock.

cast.name: Caroline
cast.impression: A Kappa with a tray of champagne and a long memory for sweatshirts. 'Bookstore boy!'

cast.name: Fitz
cast.impression: A red-faced brother in a pink tie carding freshmen with a lacrosse stick. 'Tradition!'

cast.name: Teddy Pemberton
cast.impression: Soft-faced; stands too close. He froze reciting his father's pledge class and a brother joked that his father is under oath.

cast.name: Ngozi Okafor
cast.impression: Church hat and a Tupperware with a tracking chip. She texted you: 'A Rho boy called my son's room a charity. You tell them his mother is a CPA.'

cast.name: Denise Farrow
cast.impression: Signs off 'No worries!' She emailed that your father would call at 7:30, 'between dinners', and to keep it brief.

cast.name: Mae's mother
cast.role: Cleaner, Sigma Kappa Rho (seen at dawn)
cast.impression: A small woman in a gray cleaning tunic who waxes the Rho's oak floors before the brothers wake, and dusts the glass of one old composite as if it were a child's face. Mae calls her 'Ma.'

cast.name: Assistant Trainer
cast.impression: A tired man with a tablet and a whistle he doesn't use, who looks up when a freshman hits the boards, and looks back down.

castNew.name: Mr. Dutra
castNew.impression: Seventies, cardigan, reading glasses on a chain. He has pressed the trousers of three generations of people who looked straight through him, and he says your name before you do.

castNew.name: Jess Doyle
castNew.impression: Twenty-one, counting rent in nickels behind the Anchor's bar: funny, tired, and entirely unimpressed by the name on the building up the hill. She can spot a fake from the street.

castNew.name: Gus Moretti
castNew.impression: Grey hair, forearms like hams, a laugh you hear through two floors. He knew your father when the bar was the Tap Room, and he has the stories, and a framed check, to prove it.

castNew.name: D. Rosario
castNew.impression: Dunkin' cup, reading glasses on her head, ten thousand Saturday nights behind her. Gentler than she lets on.

castNew.name: Karin Lindqvist
castNew.impression: Sunburned forearms, a Carhartt jacket in September, and nineteen hours of Interstate behind her. She shakes hands like a man and hugs like a mother.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, THIRD-FLOOR HALLWAY / CAL'S SINGLE. DAWN (SAT 09-05, 6:12 A.M.)

Friday happened offscreen, like a hangover. Cal slept fourteen hours. Priya was, as promised, very annoying: three muffins outside his door on Post-its labelled EVIDENCE OF EATING #1, #2, #3, the third with one bite out of it, initialled.
Now it's 6:12 on Saturday, the first morning of Labor Day weekend, and somebody is knocking on his door with what sounds like a bowling ball.

Tommy Reyes. Full captains'-practice sweats, sunglasses indoors, cradling a one-gallon jug of Poland Spring like a newborn. Down the side of the jug, in Sharpie, in hourly lines, the way his mother did it when he was nine: 7AM. 8AM. 9AM. And at the very bottom, in capitals: WHITAKER SAYS.
Drink water, Reyes.
He says it with enormous pride, quoting Cal's own text back to him like scripture.
My locksmith! Up at dawn!
Toast guy! Up at dawn!
Toast guy! Up at dawn!
I've drunk eleven. Eleven what, I don't know. Units.
He chugs to prove it, and misses his mouth slightly, and laughs, and wipes his chin with his sleeve.
And before you ask: both, bro. Light's fine and I'm fine. Both.
You yelled 'Worcester's finest' on Thursday. Coach heard. He thinks you're my agent.
You tried to get me benched. I forgive you. I forgive everybody before seven.
Captains' practice is at seven. The light in Kessler is personally against me. I need a witness. A spotter. A buddy.
Then, softer, almost to the jug: 'You came in the water. Nobody comes in the water.'
He squints past Cal into the single, at the radiator under the bay window, and his face does a small, happy, puzzled thing.
Since when do you have two Geralds?
A beat in which it's funny.
A beat in which it isn't.
Gerald, the only one, ticks.
Down the hall Priya's door is shut. Outside it, on the carpet, a fourth muffin, for her, from Dev, with a Post-it in his neat pre-med capitals: EAT IT.
Down the hall Priya's door is shut. Outside it, on the carpet, a fourth muffin with two Post-its, one in Dev's neat capitals and one in Cal's handwriting from last night: EAT IT.
Down the hall Priya's door is shut. Outside it, on the carpet, a fourth muffin with two Post-its, one in Dev's neat capitals and one in Cal's handwriting from last night: EAT IT.
Tommy taps the jug against Cal's chest like a toast.
Hydration king. You said never. You said drink water. I'm doing both.

choices.label: ‘Two Geralds is one too many. Health services. Today.’

reaction.text: Tommy's grin holds. It just has to hold harder.
It's Labor Day, bro. Health services is a guy named Ron and a vending machine.
He backs toward the stairs with the jug in front of him like a riot shield.
After practice. Maybe. If the light's still loud.
It's the first maybe he has ever given anyone, and he looks betrayed by his own mouth for giving it.
You said never.
I said never tell coach. I didn't say never tell you.
Lawyer.
He goes, two steps at a time, one hand on the rail the whole way down. He never uses the rail.

choices.label: ‘Two Geralds is a party. Invite me next time.’

reaction.text: Tommy laughs so hard he has to put the jug down on the carpet.
TWO GERALDS! IT'S A PARTY UP HERE!
June's door opens two inches and closes again with the soft click of a woman choosing her battles.

Tommy picks up the jug, salutes Cal with it, and thunders down the stairs. Cal stands in the doorway with the joke still in his mouth and hates how easily it came out, how perfectly it did the thing Tommy needed it to do, which was nothing.

choices.label: Take the jug. Drink with him, line for line.

reaction.text: He drinks to 7AM. Tommy drinks to 8AM. They stand in the hallway at quarter past six passing a gallon of water back and forth like two idiots at a frat party with the worst drink in the world.

reaction.paren: wiping his mouth, solemn as a priest
reaction.text: Buddy.
Buddy.
You hold it. I'll come back for it at nine. Proof of life.
He leaves the jug in Cal's arms and goes down the stairs with one hand on the rail. Tommy Reyes has never once in his life used a rail.

blocks.text: Act One · Mill Street
INT. CAL'S SINGLE, LOWELL HOUSE. MORNING (SAT 9:30 A.M.)
Priya opens his door with her hip, two Commons coffees in her hands and a blueberry muffin balanced on top of one of them, already talking.
New slippers. Yellow. Bone dry. On the record.
You knocked on Wednesday. Rude. I'm still processing it.
Yusuf says you have a photo of my feet. Delete it or frame it.
She sits cross-legged on his floor mattress, peels the muffin paper with surgical attention, and takes a bite while maintaining eye contact, like a hostage proving the food isn't poisoned.
On the record. Blueberry. Dev's checking my receipts. He has a spreadsheet. It's colour-coded. It's the most romantic thing a man has ever done for me and it isn't even romantic.
I told him before breakfast, like you said. He asked if I'd eaten. Then he made a spreadsheet. That's his love language. Columns.

She's wearing his grey St. Anselm's sweatshirt, which she stole at some point on Friday without discussing it. She is very annoying, as promised. She's also, he notices, a little shaky in the hands, the way she gets before a callback.
She pulls a single page out of the sweatshirt's front pocket, folded in four, and doesn't hand it over. She holds it flat against her chest.
You let me read one line of yours the first night. I'm letting you read one page of mine. That's the exchange rate.
You never let me read anything of yours. I'm going first anyway. That's how much I owe you.
You never let me read anything of yours. I'm going first anyway. That's how much I owe you.
You saw the title on top, last time. This time you get the whole page. I'm handing it to you. That's the difference.
You read my last draft without asking. This one I'm asking.
Mae says I have your permission retroactively. Like baptism. So this is the baptism.
She puts it face-down on the mattress between them and turns her back to him, fully, to look out his bay window at the Quad, so she won't have to watch him read.
He reads it.
THE GIRL ACROSS THE HALL (working title). A solo piece by Priya Raman. Draft 4.
LIGHTS UP. A dorm bathroom at the end of a hall. A GIRL runs the tap so nobody can hear. Across the hall, a BOY is awake. He always is. He doesn't knock. That's the deal they have.
The rest of the page is blank except for one line, crossed out and rewritten three times in three different pens: The GIRL eats a muffin like she's being watched, because she is.
No closet. The old draft opened in his closet. This one opens on the tap.
He sat outside a bathroom door for her once, on this floor, at one in the morning. Now she's written the door.
The Quad is bright and empty behind her. Her shoulders are up around her ears. She hasn't swallowed the bite of muffin. She is waiting to find out whether she can.

choices.label: ‘Who's the nobody? The one who can't hear the tap.’

reaction.text: Her back stays to him.
Everybody.
Then:
You. Dev. My mother on FaceTime, who thinks I'm a size I haven't been since ninth grade.
A long breath, in through the nose.
It's called something. I'm not saying it out loud this weekend. I wrote it down. That's a lot for one weekend.
She turns around. Her eyes are dry and furious about it.
You're allowed to knock now. New rule. I'm writing it into draft five.
She eats the rest of the muffin in four bites. Not performing it. Just eating. It's somehow much harder to watch.

choices.label: ‘Can I read the rest when there's a rest?’

reaction.text: There is no rest. It's one page. I've been writing it since Thursday. It's a very long page.
She turns around.
Yes. You can read it. First. Before Mae, before Varga, before my mother, who will think it's about a girl from Edison who isn't me.
She takes the page back, folds it in four and slides it into his sweatshirt's pocket, on her own body.
It's yours to read and mine to keep. Also a new rule.
She finishes the muffin. He watches her finish it. She lets him.

choices.label: ‘Lights up on a girl eating a muffin. Strong opening.’

reaction.text: She laughs, startled, a real one.
It IS a strong opening. Varga's going to say it's derivative of my life.
Then she takes the page back a little too fast and folds it into a very small square.
You're doing the thing. The funny thing, so it's not a thing.
A beat.
It's okay. I invented that thing. I taught it to you. I'm just saying I see it.
She eats the muffin anyway. All of it. Then she shows him the empty paper, both sides, like a magician's hand.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, THIRD-FLOOR COMMON ROOM. LATE MORNING (SAT 11:00 A.M.)

The common room, the dead ficus, Labor Day light. The floor is planning a weekend nobody will remember correctly: Simon in a camel coat he refuses to take off in September, Hunter doing calf raises for no reason, Yusuf, Priya, Dev.
Dev nods at him, easy. They survived Thursday's breakfast together.
Dev says 'Morning,' polite and a little far away, like a man waving from a boat.
Dev says 'Morning,' polite and a little far away, like a man waving from a boat.
Two things land on Cal's phone inside a minute.
The first is an email. DENISE FARROW. Subject: Tuesday!!

Your navy suit for Convocation has been sent to Alder Falls Cleaners on Mill Street for pressing. They've done Whitaker suits since your father's day! Please pick up by 3 today, they close for the holiday. Your father will be at the trustee table. He loved your 'Got it.' He says you're getting very concise!
P.S. I sent it to the cleaners because campus mail can be so unreliable! Cal, who has a photo of a forwarding card in his camera roll, reads that line twice.
P.S. Since you've changed your mail preferences, I sent it to the cleaners!
No worries! -D.
Best, Denise.
Best, Denise.
The second is a photo, from AUGIE (BUDDY): a typed list on Rho letterhead.

SATURDAY SCAVENGER · RUSHEES ONLY · DUE AT CASINO NIGHT, 9 P.M. · DRESS: FAMILY. 1. A coaster from THE ANCHOR, signed by the bartender. Not the owner. The bartender. 2. A laminated menu from Dot's. 3. A photo with a townie who calls you 'brother.' 4. A dollar from a Mill Street register. 5. Your 200m time in the river (JOKE) (UNLESS).

Colonialism with a clipboard. I'm in. Spiritually. Physically I'm at brunch.
As your guardian I forbid it. As your friend, bring me the coaster.
Hunting townies.
Item three is a hate crime against Massachusetts.
Nobody laughs at item five.

Dev doesn't say anything at all. He reads the list over Cal's shoulder and goes to refill the ficus's water, which is pointless: it has been dead since move-in. He waters it anyway, carefully, like it might still be a matter of time.
Simon, eyeing the blazer through Cal's open door: 'I'm not touching that coat again. It's haunted. By a senator.'

And on the whiteboard by the door, in Yusuf's tidy capitals, a reminder that has been there since the first week: STEAM TUNNELS · SAT 6 P.M. · WHITAKER SWORE. Underlined twice by Priya. Once by Dev. It's the promise he made the night he chose the Legacy Dinner. Next time. I swear.
And on the whiteboard by the door, in Yusuf's tidy capitals: TUNNELS II: THE RECKONING · SAT 6 P.M. · WHITAKER SWORE. Underlined twice by Priya. Once by Dev.
His father's suit is on Mill Street. His buddy's list is on Mill Street. His floor wants him underground at six.

blocks.text: INT. ALDER FALLS CLEANERS, MILL STREET. DAY (SAT 1:20 P.M.)
Mill Street on a holiday Saturday: bunting on the hardware store, a bank clock that says 88 degrees and is lying, a sign in Dot's window lettered by hand: CLOSED MON. FOR LABOR. GO HOME.

Alder Falls Cleaners, since 1958. A bell over the door. Steam. A slow carousel of plastic-sheathed clothes on a motorised track that groans as it turns. A radio on the counter tuned to oldies, playing 'Moon River', which is a joke the room doesn't know it's making.

The whole expedition crowds in behind him. Simon reads the carousel tags like a gossip column ('Pemberton. Of course Pemberton has a fur.'). Priya has her phone out and puts it away again without filming anything; she notices that she wanted to. Yusuf looks at the 1958 cash register like a man meeting his grandfather.
This is like a ride.
Behind the counter: MR. DUTRA. Seventies, cardigan, reading glasses on a chain. A man who has pressed the trousers of three generations of people who looked straight through him.

blocks.name: MR. DUTRA
blocks.text: Whitaker.
He says it before Cal says anything. He already has the garment bag down: navy, the good one, a paper tag in Denise's printing.

blocks.name: MR. DUTRA
blocks.text: Your office called ahead. Three times.
It's prepaid. He rings it up anyway, for the record, and looks at Cal over the glasses a beat longer than a man looks at a receipt.
The pink carbon receipt pad on the counter. The letterhead: ALDER FALLS CLEANERS · MILL ST. · SINCE 1958.
The same letterhead as the ticket in Cal's wallet.
It's behind the Pruitt license. It has been there since Monday. His hand finds the wallet through his jeans before he decides anything, the way it found it on Thursday when he looked at the blazer.
It's in the back fold of his wallet, alone. His hand finds the wallet through his jeans before he decides anything.
Standing at the counter, the names come up unbidden, the way they did in the chapter room. Carver. Dash. Cohen.
Two days ago he said two letters out loud and a whole room went quiet. He doesn't know why he's thinking about that now.

blocks.name: MR. DUTRA
blocks.text: We did your father's things. When he was up the hill. Rush blazers, every fall. Forty, fifty of them.
He smooths the receipt flat with two fingers.

blocks.name: MR. DUTRA
blocks.text: That week was always the worst week of the year for us.
He doesn't say why. The carousel groans around.

choices.label: Take out the 1991 ticket. Put it on the counter.

reaction.text: To get to it he has to lay Calvin R. Pruitt of Burlington, Vermont, on the counter first. Dutra looks at the license, then at Cal, and says nothing about it.
The ticket: ALDER FALLS CLEANERS · RUSH · 10/14/91 · NAVY BLAZER · STAIN: lake water.
Dutra doesn't touch it. He swaps his reading glasses for a different pair from his cardigan pocket, which is somehow worse.

reaction.name: MR. DUTRA
reaction.text: That's my father's hand. The stain line's mine. I was thirty-one.

reaction.name: MR. DUTRA
reaction.text: October that year we had a lot of blazers come in wet. Rush blazers. Lake water, every one. You can smell it. It doesn't come out of the lining. It just goes quiet.
He slides the ticket back with one finger, the way you'd hand back a photograph of somebody else's dead.

reaction.name: MR. DUTRA
reaction.text: Then we didn't. After that week nobody went in the lake for a long time.
The bell rings: a woman with a comforter. Dutra is already smiling at her.

reaction.name: MR. DUTRA

reaction.text: Dutra considers him the way you'd consider a stain. Is it set. Will it come out.

The carousel stops with a clunk at the wrong coat and he has to send it around again, and he watches it go around with his back to Cal, and that is the end of the conversation. Cal keeps his hand on his wallet the whole way out.

choices.label: Take the suit. Say thank you. Keep the ticket where it is.

reaction.text: Thanks, Mr. Dutra.
The old man blinks at his own name, which is painted on the window in gold leaf and which nobody from up the hill has said out loud in this shop in a decade.

reaction.name: MR. DUTRA
reaction.text: You're welcome, Mr. Whitaker.
Out on the sidewalk Augie holds the garment bag up by the hanger like a body.
This is what dads look like when they're not here.
He has no idea he's said anything at all. Cal touches the wallet once through the denim, a bruise check, and walks on.

blocks.text: INT. THE ANCHOR, MILL STREET. DAY (SAT 2:30 P.M.)
He has walked past this door three times in two weeks. EST. 1993 over it in chipped gold. Today he opens it.

Dark wood. A pressed-tin ceiling stained the colour of strong tea. A jukebox with a hand-lettered sign taped to the glass, NO NICKELBACK, underlined. A Red Sox day game on a television older than Cal. Four regulars at the bar who turn, all four, to look at the garment bag over his shoulder like it's a body being carried in.
A chalkboard by the taps: LABOR DAY COOKOUT · MON 4PM · TOWN ONLY · (THAT MEANS YOU, HILL).
Behind him, the expedition: Simon in his camel coat, Priya, Yusuf, and Augie holding the list in both hands like a hymnal.
Behind him, Augie, holding the list in both hands like a hymnal.
Behind him, Augie, who came anyway, holding the list in both hands like a hymnal.

Behind the bar: a woman about twenty-one, sleeves shoved up, hair in a knot with a pen through it, counting a cash drawer into exact stacks. Quarters. Dimes. Nickels. The way somebody counts when the stacks are the rent.
Two women counting coins in one week, in two different buildings, for what he suspects is the same reason. He doesn't let himself finish the sentence.
She doesn't look up.
Kitchen's closed till four. Bar's open. Coasters are not for sale.
I'm not here for the coaster.
Everybody says that.
Every year. Every single Labor Day. You'd think a two-hundred-year-old school could come up with a new list.
Augie, who has never in his life been disliked by a stranger, turns to Cal with the face of a golden retriever who's been told 'no' in a language he doesn't speak.

Priya marches to the jukebox, puts in a dollar and picks 'Glory Days' herself. A regular boos. She sings the harmony at him, badly, with total commitment, until he laughs. Simon leans on the bar and asks if they have Lillet. JESS: 'This is a bar. We have beer and regret.' SIMON: 'I'll have a regret, then. Neat.' Yusuf watches the Keno screen with professional contempt.
Augie asks for 'whatever the locals drink' and gets a Narragansett and a look.
Augie asks for 'whatever the locals drink' and gets a Narragansett and a look.
Cal orders a beer, because that's what you do. He puts the Pruitt license on the bar, because that's what he does.
She picks it up. Holds it to the window. Puts it down.
Calvin R. Pruitt of Burlington, Vermont. Who's on my phone right now in a TikTok, toasting his father. Forty thousand views. Building named after him up the hill.

The regulars enjoy this enormously. One of them applauds. On the jukebox the Boss is singing about a guy who peaked in high school, and it's suddenly about everyone in the room.

reaction.text: She looks at him properly for the first time: a fast, tired inventory, the look of someone who has carded ten thousand boys and remembers about four.
Club soda.
She pours it. Lime. Sets it on a coaster, then, very deliberately, slides the coaster out from under the glass and puts it back on the stack.
You can have the soda.
A beat.
That's two dollars. I'm not comping a Whitaker. It'd go on my permanent record.
He pays exact. Two singles, flattened. She notices. Something in her face files it in a drawer he can't see into.

choices.label: ‘Pruitt's my middle name. Spiritually.’

reaction.text: One of the regulars actually wheezes. Jess doesn't laugh. But she stops counting, which on her is the same thing.
Spiritually.
She repeats it like she's going to tell somebody about this later and wants the wording right.
Okay, Spiritual Pruitt. You get a Coke. The Coke is real. Everything else about you is pending.
She pours it. She almost smiles, and catches it like a glass going off the edge of the bar.
Don't do the voice. The charming voice. I can hear it from the street.

He pays for the Coke in exact change, quarters and a dime, counted onto the wood. He learned that this week from somebody else. Jess looks at the coins, then at him, and says nothing, which he's beginning to think is how women in this town say a lot.

choices.label: Put a fifty on the bar. ‘For the coaster. And the trouble.’

reaction.text: She looks at the fifty. She looks at him. She takes the fifty and puts it in the tip jar by the kitchen door, a pickle jar labelled DANNY'S COLLEGE FUND in a kid's handwriting gone over, years later, in adult Sharpie.
Thanks for the donation. Coaster's still not for sale.
She goes back to counting nickels. The regulars aren't laughing anymore. They're watching him the way you'd watch a dog that just bit somebody, waiting to see whose it is.
That's the thing about you guys. You think the trouble has a price.

blocks.text: INT. THE ANCHOR. DAY (SAT 2:50 P.M.)
The kitchen door bangs open.

DANNY DOYLE, seventeen, Dot's apron still on from the breakfast shift, backpack over one shoulder, earbuds in, heading for the back office with the purposeful slouch of a kid who has a lot of homework and none of it is homework.
He sees Cal at the bar.
His face does three things very fast. Delight. Recognition. Terror.

blocks.name: DANNY
blocks.text: PRUITT!

blocks.name: DANNY
blocks.text: Hey! Vermont guy! The one who didn't buy!
Jess turns. Slowly. The way you turn toward a sound in a house at night.
You know him?
Danny's eyes go to the license still lying on the bar under Cal's hand: the glossy laminate, Dot's menu stock, his own work. Then to his sister. He's seventeen and it shows. He has no plan.
Danny's eyes go to Cal, then to his sister. He's seventeen and it shows. He has no plan.
Then to the tip jar, where a fifty is sitting on top of the singles. 'Dude,' he says, to the fifty, to Cal, and can't decide whether to be grateful or insulted, and settles on both, like his sister.
The backpack is unzipped an inch. Cal can see the corner of a laptop inside. Brand new. The protective film still on the lid.
Jess sees Cal see it.
A regular at the end of the bar, to nobody: 'Here we go.' On the television the Red Sox strand two runners. Nobody in the room is watching.
Hey! Are you a townie? Can you call me brother? It's for a list.
Danny looks at Augie with naked pity.
At the jukebox Priya narrates under her breath to Simon, nature-documentary hush: 'The young male approaches the watering hole.' Simon: 'Shh. The young one is about to be eaten.'
Jess is still waiting. She has her brother's face, older, more tired, and she is reading Cal and Danny both, and she is good at it. She just doesn't have the piece Cal has.
Danny's eyes on Cal are begging, in the plainest language there is, for one more lie.

choices.label: ‘He sold me a grilled cheese. At Dot's. Great grilled cheese.’

reaction.text: Danny exhales like a tyre.

reaction.name: DANNY
reaction.text: Best grilled cheese in the Berkshires. Ask anybody.
He doesn't make the grilled cheese. Dot makes the grilled cheese.

reaction.name: DANNY
reaction.text: I sell it, though. Presentation.
Jess looks between them for a long second. She lets it go, which is not the same thing as believing it, and Cal knows the difference because it's his specialty.
Danny, passing behind him to the office, doesn't look at him at all. From a seventeen-year-old, that's a thank-you note.

choices.label: Tell Jess the truth: ‘He made my license.’

reaction.text: The bar goes quiet in a way the Red Sox can't fix.

Danny goes white, then red. Jess doesn't look at Danny. She picks up the license, turns it over, runs her thumb along the edge and finds the faint ridge where the menu laminate overlaps, and her face closes like a door in wind.
Office. Now.
He goes. She puts the license face-down on the bar and pushes it back to Cal with two fingers.
You didn't have to buy it. That's the part I'll remember. Not that he sold it. That you bought it.
She follows Danny into the back. The door shuts. The regulars look at Cal like he's a fire alarm.

choices.label: Say nothing. Let Danny find his own way out.

reaction.text: Cal drinks his drink. Danny stands there with nothing.

reaction.name: DANNY
reaction.text: Customer. From Dot's. He tips bad.
He walks to the office. Jess watches him go, then watches Cal, who has turned the license face-down under his glass.
You tip bad. Is that true?
It's true today.
She almost laughs. She isn't done with either of them. He can tell by the way she goes back to counting from the very beginning of the stack.

blocks.text: INT. THE ANCHOR, BY THE REGISTER / THE FRONT WINDOW. DAY (SAT 3:10 P.M.)

The office door opens. Jess comes back out alone, her face shut like a till, and goes to the taps without looking at Cal. Through the gap behind her, Danny at a desk with his head in his hands. She pulls the door to.

A trapdoor behind the bar thumps open and GUS MORETTI comes up out of the cellar with a keg on his shoulder like a sleeping kid. Fifty-five. Grey hair, forearms like hams, a laugh you can hear through two floors before you've seen the man.
He sets the keg down. Sees the garment bag. Sees the face. And does what nobody else in this town has done all day. He grins.
Whitaker. Like the building, right? I've heard you say it. Everybody's heard you say it. You've got the jaw. Christ. Hang on.
Cal. Just Cal. Sure. And I'm just Gus. You've got the jaw, kid. Christ. Hang on.
He reaches behind the register, past the Keno slips, and taps a small, cheap frame on the wall beside the liquor license.

Inside it: a personal check, yellowed. PAY TO THE ORDER OF Gus. FORTY DOLLARS AND 00/100. Signed in a hand Cal knows from every birthday card he ever got that wasn't really from his father. Richard C. Whitaker. October 1990.
Your father bet me he could drink a yard of ale faster than a townie. He couldn't. Wrote me a check. I never cashed it.
The grin widens.
Leverage.
The regulars roar. It gets better every time.
Building was the Tap Room then. I just carried the kegs. Same kegs. Same stairs. Worse knees.
Convocation suit. Your father wore one just like it. Spilled a whole pitcher down it on this exact spot.
Tell Brooks Hadley the coasters are twenty bucks this year. Inflation.
Tell Brooks Hadley the coasters are twenty bucks this year. Inflation.
He pays exact.
He pays exact.
Huh. Not like his old man.
Huh. Not like his old man.
He tips in fifties.
Now that's his old man.
Then Augie, still working the list, desperate to give anybody anything:
Sir, is there any way I could get a photo on the water? Like a lake photo? For the list?

I don't do the lake.
Pleasant. Final. The way a man says he doesn't eat shellfish. He picks the keg back up, though it doesn't need moving.

Through the front window, Mill Street. Dev is on the sidewalk outside, in a grey Whitlock T-shirt, early for meeting the floor, with his hands in his pockets. Priya waves at him through the glass to come in. He doesn't come in. He looks past her, at Gus, and Gus looks at him, and each of them lifts a hand, the small exact nod of two men who have sat in the same room many times.
Priya, at the door: 'Do you know that guy?' Dev: 'Everybody knows Gus.' Which isn't an answer. Gus watches him to the corner.

Through the front window, Mill Street: a runner in a grey Whitlock T-shirt goes past with his earbuds in. Dev. He sees Gus through the glass, and Gus sees him, and each of them lifts a hand, the small exact nod of two men who have sat in the same room many times.

Then Gus looks back at Cal, who saw it. And Gus's eyes do the thing a reporter's do.
INT. CAL'S SINGLE, LOWELL HOUSE. EVENING (SAT 5:40 P.M.)
The navy suit hangs on the closet door where the blazer hung on Thursday. The blazer has been moved to the back of the closet, which feels like a demotion it will report to someone.
On the desk, the gallon jug. 9AM has not been crossed out. Tommy never came back for it. Cal notices that, and puts the jug where he'll stop noticing it, and keeps noticing it.
A Narragansett coaster, signed in ballpoint: GO HOME - J.
Priya's phone, earlier, in the Lowell stairwell: a photo of Augie holding a coaster signed GO HOME - J. like a diploma. 'He thinks it's a nickname,' Priya had said. 'Nobody tell him. Ever.'

msgs.text: even #3!! a guy called me brother but then he said a bad word after it

blocks.text: At 5:40 the door opens without a knock.

Priya in a miner's helmet with the lamp switched on. Yusuf with the 1974 blueprint rolled under his arm like a field marshal. Dev with a backpack of granola bars and a first-aid kit. Simon, last, in a floor-length black cape he insists is a coat.
Six o'clock. You swore. In front of a ficus.
Six o'clock. You've been under once. This is the sequel. Sequels are mandatory.
You promised me tomorrow on Thursday. I'm collecting.
Before you answer, know that I've worn this for you. It has a lining.
Two hours. Maybe three. Depends who panics.
Nobody panics. I brought granola.
At the same moment his phone, twice.

blocks.text: And under it, at last, an answer to the text he sent her in the small hours of Friday. He had decided she wasn't going to answer it.

msgs.text: You looked like you meant it.
Casino Night. I'm dealing blackjack. Come early if you want to watch me count.

blocks.text: Three invitations. One of them is a promise he made nine days ago and broke the same night.
The lamp on Priya's helmet is pointed directly into his eyes. She doesn't move it.

reaction.text: Priya screams. Dev hands him a granola bar and a headlamp without a word, like a nurse handing a surgeon a scalpel.
Yusuf unrolls the blueprint across Cal's desk and taps an X drawn in pencil under the Commons.
Entry's behind Lowell's boiler room. Exit's wherever we survive.
Simon swirls the cape. Cal texts Augie.

msgs.text: Meet you at 9. Inside. Save me a seat.

reaction.text: A pirate flag, which feels like an omen and probably isn't.

choices.label: ‘Raincheck. Augie needs a buddy at the pregame.’

reaction.text: Priya's lamp drops, slowly, like a sun going down.
Raincheck. Like it's raining.
Dev puts a hand on her shoulder.
Buddy system's a real thing, Pree.
He means it. It costs him something to mean it. Yusuf rolls up the blueprint without comment and, on the way out, adds a line to the whiteboard: WHITAKER SWORE (2).
Cal puts on the blazer, not the suit. DRESS: FAMILY. It still knows his shoulders. He goes down the hill to Elm Row and feels the whole floor at his back the entire way.
Cal puts on the Rho quarter-zip again. DRESS: FAMILY. He goes down the hill to Elm Row and feels the whole floor at his back the entire way.
Cal puts on the black sweater again. DRESS: FAMILY. He goes down the hill to Elm Row and feels the whole floor at his back the entire way.

choices.label: ‘Go without me. I want to watch her count.’

reaction.text: Her.
Just that. The helmet lamp stays on his face for one second longer.
Okay. Go watch her count.
She turns and goes, and the others follow. Simon, last, holding the cape in one hand, stops in the door.
You keep going places with your whole body, Calvin, and leaving your face here.
The whiteboard gets a second line: WHITAKER SWORE (2).
He goes to Elm Row with the blazer on and the feeling he's left something on the stove.
He goes to Elm Row in the quarter-zip with the feeling he's left something on the stove.
He goes to Elm Row in the black sweater with the feeling he's left something on the stove.

blocks.text: INT. STEAM TUNNELS UNDER THE QUAD. NIGHT (SAT 6:15-8:30 P.M.)
Behind Lowell's boiler room, a steel door that Yusuf opens with a library card and a look of mild regret.

blocks.paren: to Cal, on the stairs down
blocks.text: I'm off the case. I don't do cases anymore. Cases do me.

blocks.paren: to Cal, on the stairs down
blocks.text: You never said anything. She did. That's better.

blocks.paren: to Cal, on the stairs down
blocks.text: You never said anything. She did. That's better.

Then down. Heat like a held breath. Pipes wrapped in asbestos-era cloth. The hum of the whole university's plumbing. A century of graffiti in flashlight: CLASS OF '58 WAS HERE. MARLOWE PLAYERS 1977 LIVE FOREVER. A heart around two sets of initials, one of them scratched out by somebody else.
Priya's lamp swings across all of it like a lighthouse with ADHD. Simon narrates as a Victorian explorer.
The natives have left us this crude depiction of a phallus. We shall name it Pruitt.

Yusuf navigates by blueprint, counting steps out loud. Dev brings up the rear, the sweep, making sure nobody's left behind, handing out granola bars on a schedule only he knows. Once, Priya takes one before she's handed it and eats it, walking. Dev doesn't say a word. His whole body says thank you.

In a stretch where Priya's lamp is off, she says to nobody in particular: 'I like it down here. Nobody can see what you eat.' Then the lamp comes back on, bright, and she's already talking about something else.

Under the Commons the tunnel widens into a brick vault where the steam mains cross. The ceiling's lower here. Cal's head is a foot from the pipes. Through the brick overhead: the dining hall. Chairs, a dishwasher, a dropped tray, three hundred people eating dinner under his grandfather's portrait.

blocks.paren: glancing up at the dishwasher noise
blocks.text: Daddy's dining hall. Secret lottery.
Retired. That bit's retired.
And on the far wall of the vault, older than everything around it, stencilled in paint gone the colour of dried blood, letters a foot high, one word to a course of brick:
THE LAKE KEEPS.
Nobody says anything. The pipes knock twice, like Gerald's cousin.

blocks.paren: quietly, for once without a bit
blocks.text: Every school has a lake that keeps things. Ours just has better PR.
Then he's silent for two full seconds, which for Simon is a medical event, and then he over-performs his way out of it, loudly, about the acoustics.

blocks.paren: running a fingertip beside the paint, not on it
blocks.text: Early nineties. Lead-based. Don't lick it.
Priya turns her lamp off. In the dark you can hear Dev breathing, steady and slow, the way you breathe when you've had to learn how.

choices.label: Photograph it. ‘Collector,’ like Brooks said.

reaction.text: The flash fills the vault and everyone yells.
THE LAKE KEEPS sits in his camera roll now, two swipes from the empty oval and the forwarding card and the roster. A family album of things nobody explained to him.
THE LAKE KEEPS sits in his camera roll now, two swipes from the forwarding card and the roster. A family album of things nobody explained to him.
You've got a folder.
He has a folder. Simon, watching Cal look at his phone, says nothing, which is unusual enough that Cal notices, and doesn't ask why.

choices.label: ‘Keeps what?’ Ask the dark.

reaction.text: Nobody answers, because nobody knows. That's the answer.
Secrets. Obviously. It's a lake. It's a metaphor. Every lake is.
Bodies.
He says it before he can stop it, the way you say a word in your sleep. Then, fast:
Joke. Rowing ghosts. Everybody's got a rowing ghost.

Priya's lamp comes back on and it's on Dev's face, and Dev's face is perfectly fine. Too fine. Cal reads it, files it, and lets it go, because Dev is owed one and Cal isn't going to collect it in a tunnel.

choices.label: Put your palm flat under the letters. Keep walking.

reaction.text: The brick is warm from the pipes, like something alive. He doesn't know why he does it. Priya watches him do it and doesn't film it. He notices she doesn't. She notices him notice.
Come on. Exit's under Fennimore. If we're right. If we're wrong, it's under the president's house and we're expelled.

They come up through a grate behind Fennimore at 8:30 into the evening air, filthy and laughing. Simon swirls the cape and declares them a secret society, and for ten whole minutes it is the best night Cal has had at Whitlock.

blocks.text: INT. SIGMA KAPPA RHO, THE BACK PARLOR. EVENING (SAT 7:10 P.M.)

The Rho's back parlour is being turned into Monte Carlo by eight freshmen and a lot of green felt rented from a party store in Pittsfield. Fitz is up a stepladder hanging a disco ball, crooked, with the focus of a surgeon.
Two of the freshmen setting up chips whisper as Cal passes: 'That's the guy from the lawn.'
At the far table, alone, in a black dress and the pearls from Thursday, Margaux Vance is shuffling a six-deck shoe.
Not like a sorority girl at a theme party. Like a professional. Riffle, bridge, cut, one-handed, the cards falling into each other with a sound like light rain.
She doesn't look up.
You came early to watch me count. Most men come late to watch me lose.
He sits across from her. She deals him a hand face up, out of habit. Seventeen.
Stand. You always want to hit on seventeen. Everybody does. That's how the house pays for the felt.

Up close, in the parlour's yellow light, the dress is last season's and has been taken in at the waist by hand. Tiny stitches. Not a tailor's. At her elbow, an envelope: KAPPA LAMBDA · DEALER FEE · $100, in round, careful handwriting that isn't hers.
They pay dealers. A hundred dollars and a corsage. The corsage is for the photos.
A store tag. A coin purse. A nickel. Now stitches and an envelope. He has a list now, too. He hates that it looks like hers.
He sees the stitches. He doesn't know what they mean.
She deals herself a card face down and doesn't look at it.
I learned at a hospital gala in Greenwich when I was nine. My father taught me. It's the only thing he ever taught me that was true.
She says it lightly. Her hands keep shuffling. They don't stop once.

choices.label: Watch her hands. Say: ‘You don't stop. Ever.’

reaction.text: Her hands stop.

Mid-riffle. Half the deck in each palm, a little bridge of cards arched between them, held. It's the first time he's seen her body do something she didn't decide to do. She looks down at her own hands like they belong to someone she's babysitting.
If I stop, I'll count something else.
She finishes the shuffle. Perfect.
Don't tell anyone I said that. Especially me.
BEAUTIFUL.
The disco ball falls.

choices.label: Lean across the felt and kiss her. Pledges watching.

reaction.text: She lets him, over the shoe, for exactly as long as it takes Fitz to notice and start a slow clap that the freshmen join because they don't know what else to do.
Special Collections, a week ago: a librarian's cough. Tonight the cough is a slow clap. Progress, of a kind.
She sits back and deals the next card without looking.
Now it's a picture.
A beat.
Again.

And it's lovely, and it's a performance, and he can't tell which, and he can tell that she can't either. Her hand on the shoe isn't quite steady. The envelope with $100 on it is very steady, under her elbow, where it has been all along.

choices.label: ‘That's the problem, you said. What's the problem?’

reaction.text: She deals him a card. An ace, beside a king. Blackjack. She pays him a chip he never bet.
The problem is that I meant it on the lawn, and I'd have done it anyway if I hadn't, and I can't tell you why I'd have done it anyway.
She gathers the cards.
Ask me in daylight sometime. Not here. Everything in this house is a little bit listening.
She glances, very briefly, up at the corner of the ceiling, at a smoke detector, the way you'd glance at someone across a party. He looks too. It's a smoke detector. It's nothing.

blocks.text: Act Two · The House
INT. SIGMA KAPPA RHO, 14 ELM ROW: THE BACK PARLOR AND FOYER. CASINO NIGHT. NIGHT (SAT 9:00-11:30 P.M.)
Rush, night three. The moose head in the foyer wears a green dealer's visor. The disco ball is back up, crooked. 'Poker Face' is on a loop because a brother thinks it's thematic.

Rushees in DRESS: FAMILY, one kid in his grandfather's kilt, lose plastic chips at roulette and at a corner table called the Bank, where the house lends you chips. Every chip you can't pay back by eleven is a shot.
Cal arrives at nine with soot on his cuff and brick dust in his hair. Margaux, dealing, doesn't look up: 'You've been underground.'
Cal arrives at nine from the annex, where he watched Augie do three shots of something blue 'for the energy' and then hug a brother he'd met that minute.
Cal has been in the parlour since seven, watching the brothers take their positions like a crew before a heist.
At the door Brooks pins a little gold loving cup to Cal's lapel, the pin every signed legacy wears tonight, and rests a hand on his shoulder the way a hand Cal knows rests there in photographs.
At the door Brooks looks at Cal's empty lapel, where the signed legacies wear a little gold pin. 'Still sleeping on it?'
At the door Brooks lets him in as Augie's guest. 'Nobody walks out the first night. They walk back in.'
Gentlemen. The swimmer. Buoy and back, at night, drunk. And then again, for a hockey player. The only legacy in this house who goes in after people.
Gentlemen. The swimmer. Buoy and back, at night, drunk.
Gentlemen. The swimmer. Buoy and back, at night, drunk.
Gentlemen. The swimmer. Went in after a hockey player on Thursday. The only legacy in this house who goes in after people.
Gentlemen. The legacy.
It sticks instantly.
Any more letters tonight, swimmer?
Hollis, gentle in a dinner jacket, holds Cal's handshake a beat too long.
I asked Brooks about the letters. He said house ghost. Brooks doesn't believe in ghosts.
Brooks says you knew every name. Every single one.
Brooks says you knew every name. Every single one.
This guy called the Rho a cult with a merchandise table. To Brooks's FACE.
Marcus at the cashier's window, logging every chip.
Tommy, in the same too-small borrowed blazer, swigs clear liquid from a Tanqueray bottle labelled in Sharpie: WHITAKER SAYS. It's water, he tells everyone. Mostly, it is.
Hydration. Like you said.
Hydration. Like you said.
He sits down hard on the stairs once, laughing, and gets up slower than a man his age should.
He sits down hard on the stairs once, laughing, and gets up slower than a man his age should.
He tells three brothers about the two Geralds and they laugh until they cry, and he laughs too, and squeezes his right eye shut when nobody's looking but Cal.
Near her blackjack table the brothers part for Cal like he's married.
Margaux deals under the disco ball with the face of a woman reading a grocery list, and beats everyone.
When he passes her table, her hands stop for half a second. Then go on.
On the way to the bathroom at ten he passes the 1991-92 composite. The glass is spotless. He doesn't look. He looks.
At 11:02 Hollis's phone lights in his jacket. He excuses himself 'to take a call' and goes upstairs, and doesn't come back.
And Augie. At the Bank, in his father's tie, losing. Not a little. Every chip. He keeps borrowing.
My family's good for it!
It's a joke. His face when he says it isn't.
At 10:40 he takes off his watch, the one too good for his shoes, and pushes it across the felt.
That's collateral.
The brothers love it. Six little paper cups of something brown line up in front of him. Augie looks for Cal across the room.
Buddy system.

reaction.text: He walks over and drops his stack on the felt, the black stack every legacy was handed at the door.
Whitaker's good for it.
The brothers cheer the name. Augie's watch slides back across the felt. Augie hugs him so hard Cal's ribs click.

Then the brothers line up the shots anyway. The chips don't cancel the shots. Nothing cancels the shots. And Augie, so grateful he can't stand still, drinks three of them to say thank you. Cal drinks two of his.
Paying for things. Very on brand.

choices.label: Pull Augie out of the game. ‘Buddy. Air. Now.’

reaction.text: Augie comes like a dog called off a road, so relieved it's almost funny.

On the back porch, in the cold, he talks for ten minutes about combines, about his little sister's 4-H heifer, about the smell of a shop floor at six in the morning, and doesn't once mention money. So carefully that Cal hears all of it.

reaction.name: A BROTHER
reaction.text: Lindqvist! You owe the Bank six!
Just gonna settle up, buddy. It's an honour thing.
He's back inside before Cal can stop him. The screen door slaps shut behind him like a punchline nobody laughs at.

choices.label: Leave him. Go sit at Margaux's table.

reaction.text: He tells himself Augie's a grown man. He sits down at the blackjack table. Margaux deals him in without looking up.
Your friend at the Bank is doing a very expensive impression of you.
He laughs. She doesn't.
He plays four hands. He wins three, because she lets him, and he knows she lets him. When he looks back at the Bank at 11:15, Augie isn't there.

blocks.text: INT. SIGMA KAPPA RHO, SECOND-FLOOR BATHROOM. NIGHT (SAT 11:43 P.M.)
Tommy's voice on the stairs. Too loud. Wrong.
WHITAKER. Your buddy.
The second-floor bathroom. Black-and-white tile from 1920. A clawfoot tub full of ice and empty cans. A mirror with a crack across it in the shape of Florida.
Augie is on the floor between the tub and the toilet, on his back, in his father's tie.

His lips are the wrong colour. His skin is cold and wet, like something left out in the rain. His breathing is slow, then slower, and then there's a gap where breathing should be, and then a ragged catch.

Tommy is kneeling in the mess beside him, patting his cheek, 'Buddy, buddy, buddy,' squinting, seeing two of everything. Brothers jammed in the doorway. Fitz with both hands in his hair. Somebody already holding a phone up, then thinking better of it.
Augie's eyes open a slit and find Cal. 'Buddy.' Cal left the Bank. Cal sat at a card table and won three hands he was given.
Three of those shots were a thank-you. Cal paid for the watch. Augie paid for the thank-you.
He got him out once. Augie went back in to settle up.
Buddy system. Never drink without a buddy. Augie's voice, from the lawn.
Then Brooks, through the crowd. Calm. Perfect suit, perfect voice. A man who has been in this room before.
Okay. Okay. On his side. Recovery position. Bucket. Somebody sits with him. We wait it out.
He kneels and rolls Augie onto his side with practised hands. Then he starts counting Augie's breaths, under his own breath.
In. Four. Hold. Out, eight.
Cal has seen those words, carved low in the wainscot of a Lowell closet room: B.H. '28 · 4 IN. HOLD. 8 OUT. He knows what they are now.
Four in. Hold. Eight out. It isn't for Augie. It's too practised to be for Augie.
Four in. Hold. Eight out. It isn't for Augie. It's too practised to be for Augie.
With the lights on. Every light. He understands, now, what the breathing is for.
Brooks stands. To the doorway:

Nobody calls anyone. You call, the house is done, rush is done, he's done. He gets written up and loses his aid, and you lose everything you came here for. He drank alone in his room before. He came to us. That's what happened.

blocks.text: INT. PRUITT HALL, HERALD BASEMENT. NIGHT (SUN 7:30 P.M.)

The Herald on a holiday Sunday. One desk lamp on. A century of framed front pages on the walls, the 1994 Commons groundbreaking among them. A police scanner on a shelf murmuring Alder Falls to itself. The editor's door shut, light under it, typing.

Nora at her desk, a Fennimore circulation-desk lanyard still around her neck from a double shift, eating cold lo mein out of the carton with a pencil. Her corkboard, door-sized, still under the flowered bedsheet, tacked at all four corners.
She doesn't stand up. She turns her laptop around.
RHO PLEDGE HOSPITALIZED; RUSH SUSPENDED. By Nora Castellanos. Convocation issue, Tuesday.

She has built it like a clock. Fitz's Instagram story, 11:41 p.m.: Augie upright at the Bank with a paper cup. The Public Safety log, public by law. The scanner, which she listens to the way other people listen to podcasts. The dean's email, which Simon forwarded to half the campus by 1:10.
The scanner caught the dispatcher repeating it back. 'Caller is a Calvin Whitaker.' You said your own name to a dispatcher. Out loud. On Elm Row.

No 911 from the house. A Range Rover registered to a Hadley family trust in the ER bay at 12:16, per a nurse who likes the Herald. And Fitz's story at 11:52: you, carrying him down the back stairs by the legs.
And a 911 from the car. From a Margaux Vance.
She says the name with no inflection at all.

Fitz's story at 11:41: him upright. The 911 at 12:14, from a Marcus Bell. Thirty-three minutes. Somebody posted the bathroom door at 11:52 with a caption I won't read you. What happened in thirty-three minutes?
And one gap she can't close without him.
You were there. You were on four people's stories. You were in the bathroom.
Not a question. She puts down the pencil. Her voice is level. Her hands on the desk, either side of the laptop, aren't doing anything at all, which on Nora is like someone else shaking.
I need one thing. The call. Who made it, and when. I'm asking on the record. I'll take it on background. I'll take no comment.
A beat.
I'm not asking as your partner. I'm asking as the person whose job this is.
She pushes a page across the desk: his pencil, Not reading under it, her green Noted. 'I'm asking you to read under this one,' she says. 'Yours. Not mine.'
You wrote about a call you made when you were eleven. I read it. You know what a call costs. That's why I asked you and not Fitz.
My father called. First time since I got here.
My father left me a voicemail. First time since I got here.
She says nothing about his father. In her notebook, angled where he can't see it, she writes a single line: R.W. called. 1st time.

She says it like a joke. It isn't shaped like one.
She has chapter at eight. She stands, brushes off her cardigan, and looks down at him on the slate.

Cal.

Augie in a wheelchair he doesn't need, in grey sweatpants from the gift shop with BERKSHIRE MEDICAL down one leg. Pale. Hungover in a way that goes all the way to the bone. Grinning when he sees Cal, then wincing at grinning.

Beside him, KARIN LINDQVIST. Fifties. Sunburned forearms. A Carhartt jacket in September. Reading glasses pushed up into hair the colour of wheat. A face that drove nineteen hours without stopping, except for gas and the bathroom and once, she says, to cry at a rest stop in Ohio 'for exactly ten minutes. I timed it.'
She shakes Cal's hand like a man, and then pulls him in and hugs him like a mother.

Cal opens his mouth and doesn't have an answer. Augie sees that he doesn't, and nods like that's an answer, and goes. Cal stays on the steps with the question, which is better than any answer he could have given. And much worse.

blocks.text: INT. PRUITT HALL, HERALD BASEMENT. NIGHT (MON 09-07, 9:00 P.M.)
The Herald basement, nine p.m., Labor Day. The editor's door is open now, the office behind it empty. On the desk, Nora's draft, with a red Sharpie line through one paragraph.
Nora alone with the proof of the Convocation issue. Page one, below the fold: RHO PLEDGE HOSPITALIZED; RUSH SUSPENDED.
The pull quote, in bold: 'Somebody said nobody calls anyone,' said Calvin Whitaker, the freshman who placed the 911 call at 11:47 p.m. 'He was breathing six times a minute. I called.'
The pull quote, in bold: 'We were told no sirens,' said Calvin Whitaker, the freshman who drove the pledge to Berkshire Medical. 'So nobody called from the house. That was wrong.'
The pull quote, in bold: 'It was thirty-one minutes,' said Calvin Whitaker, a freshman who was in the room. 'I was counting. I should have been calling.'
Fourth paragraph: A source with knowledge of the events said a member of the house told those present that 'nobody calls anyone.'
Sixth paragraph: Calvin Whitaker, a legacy rushee present in the bathroom, declined to comment.
The scanner murmurs. She eats the last of the lo mein cold.
Then she gets up and untacks the bedsheet over the corkboard. One corner. Two. Three. Four. She lets it fall.

All of it, in this light. The 1991-92 Rho composite printout with its empty oval. The Polaroid of a young man on a dock: Tomas, Tamsin Lake, oct. 1991. The index card from the first night: WHO WAS ON THE DOCK? The Herald's 1994 front page: the Whitaker Commons groundbreaking. A map of the lake with the Rho dock and the boathouse circled in green.

The navy suit back on its hanger on the closet door, the tie still knotted, Priya's knot, hung over the neck of the hanger like a noose somebody tied with love.
